newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rescue raid launched from carpeted tunnels.
newsitem.headline: Peru rescue raid launched from carpeted tunnels.

text.p: The intricate warren of tunnels used to launch a surprise attack on Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima were spacious, well-lit and even carpeted, television images showed on Friday.

The exclusive footage by Peru's America television network showed the short President Alberto Fujimori stooping slightly as he walked along the corridors from which scores of crack troops sprang out to rescue the hostages and kill the rebels.
The tunnels, where commandos waited for more than a day for the order to strike, were built during the 18-week siege under the cover of martial anthems blasted from loudspeakers outside.
Walled by sturdy planks and illuminated by strip lights, the corridors had standing ventilators spaced at regular intervals and sections furnished with red carpet.

Fujimori was accompanied on his inspection tour by military commandos wearing black ski masks. Other images showed Fujimori huddled with the soldiers over maps of the diplomatic compound and the tunnel complex.
In another segment, the Peruvian leader used a rope to pull himself up a ladder leading to the surface.
In a detailed account of the assault that saved all but one of the 72 hostages, Fujimori said on Wednesday troops used at least five tunnels, with numerous exits, to swarm into the mansion.

One tunnel led right up beneath the home's reception room, where at the time of the attack several rebels were playing soccer with a ball improvised from socks wrapped in tape. Five guerrillas were killed instantly by an explosion at this tunnel's mouth, which signalled the start of the raid, Fujimori told Reuters on Friday.

The tunnels were excavated over two months by specialised miners recruited in the Peruvian Andes, according to a local newspaper report on Friday. Two miners died, buried alive, when part of one tunnel collapsed, the pro-government Expreso newspaper said.
Two army officers and all 14 of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were killed in Tuesday's assault that ended the 126-day-old standoff.
